publishedSummary: Arterial pressure is defended on two timescales: a neural reflex that acts within seconds, and hormonal control that acts over hours to days. Measuring it accurately is a third problem, and most errors at the bedside are errors of technique rather than of physiology.

sections.narrative:
The fastest control of arterial pressure is neural, and it begins with sensors in the walls of the great arteries. Arterial baroreceptors are stretch receptors located mainly in the carotid sinus and the aortic arch, positioned where they can sample the pressure of blood heading for the brain and for the body. They do not measure pressure directly; they respond to the stretch that pressure imposes on the arterial wall, and their firing rate rises and falls with it. Afferents from the carotid sinus travel in the glossopharyngeal nerve, while aortic-arch baroreceptor afferents travel in the aortic nerve and the vagus nerve to the brainstem.

Because firing is continuous and proportional, the reflex works in both directions from a set point. A rise in pressure increases baroreceptor discharge, which inhibits sympathetic outflow and increases vagal tone, slowing the heart and dilating vessels until pressure falls. A fall in pressure reduces discharge and releases the opposite response. The loop operates beat to beat, which is what allows arterial pressure to be held stable through a change of posture. Its limitation is the mirror image of its strength: because it works from a set point that resets over time, it defends against sudden change but does not determine the long-term level of blood pressure.

The same efferent machinery can be driven centrally rather than by the baroreceptors, and then the pattern of response changes character. An acute threatening stimulus can raise heart rate and arterial pressure, increase skeletal-muscle blood flow, and simultaneously constrict splanchnic, renal and cutaneous vessels. This is not simple global vasoconstriction — it is a redistribution, moving blood toward the muscles that might be used and away from beds whose perfusion can safely be deferred. Recognising it as redistribution rather than as a pressure response explains why the skin becomes pale and cold while pressure and muscle flow both rise.

Arterial blood pressure is the lateral pressure exerted by flowing blood on the arterial wall. The word lateral matters: the quantity measured is the outward push against the wall, not the forward force driving flow along the vessel, which is why pressure can be measured from outside the artery at all.

That is exactly what a cuff does. Inflating a cuff around the arm applies external pressure to the tissues and, through them, to the brachial artery. When cuff pressure exceeds systolic arterial pressure, the artery is occluded throughout the cardiac cycle, no blood passes, and Korotkoff sounds are absent — silence above systolic pressure is not a failure to hear but the expected finding. As the cuff is released below systolic pressure, blood begins to spurt through the partly compressed artery in turbulent bursts, and those bursts are the sounds. When cuff pressure falls below diastolic, flow becomes continuous and laminar again, and the sounds disappear once more.

The technique's dependence on transmitting cuff pressure faithfully to the artery is where it fails. A cuff applied too loosely does not transmit its pressure efficiently to the underlying tissues, so it must be inflated well beyond the true arterial pressure before the artery is occluded — and the reading is falsely high. The same logic accounts for the error from a cuff that is too narrow for the arm. In both cases the fault is in the coupling between cuff and artery, and the error is in the same direction, which makes it predictable and therefore avoidable.

Where the baroreflex acts in seconds, hormonal control acts over hours and days, and its central agent is angiotensin II. Angiotensin II raises arterial pressure through vasoconstriction and increased sympathetic activity — two mechanisms operating on the same variable from different directions.

The direct action is on vascular smooth muscle, where angiotensin II is among the most potent constrictors known, raising total peripheral resistance. The indirect action is neural: it augments sympathetic outflow and facilitates noradrenaline release at nerve terminals, so the same neural signal produces a greater vascular response. To these is added a slower, volume-based effect, since angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone release and promotes sodium and water retention, raising the volume the heart has to pump.

That combination — immediate constriction, amplified sympathetic tone, and sustained volume expansion — is what makes this system the long-term regulator that the baroreflex is not. It is also why interrupting it pharmacologically lowers pressure by several mechanisms at once, and why the same pathway that defends pressure in haemorrhage becomes damaging when it is chronically activated in a patient who is not volume-depleted.
